message.content: I heard, then, that near Naukratis in Egypt there lived one of the old gods of that place, to whom also the bird is dedicated that is called Ibis. And the god himself was said to be called Teut. He was said to have first invented numbers and calculations, geometry and astronomy, further draughts and the game of dice, and besides that, letters. King of all Egypt at that time was Tamuz, and he reigned in that great city in Upper Egypt which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and the god they call Ammon. To him, then, came Teut, taught him his arts and told him to spread them among the other Egyptians. And he asked what benefit each of them would bring, and then, as Teut's words seemed to him right or not right, he blamed one thing and praised another. About each art Tamuz had much good and much bad to say to Teut, which it would take long to relate. Now when they came to letters, Teut said to Tamuz: "King, this learning will make the Egyptians wiser and more capable in remembering; this invention is a remedy for memory and wisdom." And he said to him in answer: "Teut, most perfect master! One is able to beget what belongs to an art, and another is able to judge for what it may be useful and in what harmful to those who will want to make use of the given art. So also now: you are the father of letters, therefore out of good heart for them you have ascribed to them a value directly opposite to the one which they really possess. This invention will sow forgetfulness in human souls, because a man who learns this will stop exercising memory; he will trust writing and will recall everything from outside, from signs foreign to his being, and not from his own inside, from himself. So this is not a remedy for memory, only a means for recalling to oneself. To your pupils you will give only a semblance of wisdom, and not true wisdom. For they will possess great well-readness without learning, and it will seem to them that they know much, and for the most part they will know nothing, and it will only be hard to associate with them; these will be sages in appearance, and not people wise in truth."
